messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: vtest screencast
parts:
Hi everyone -

I created a screencast for setting up and using vtest with ggplot2 here:
http://ascii.io/a/383

In the screencasts, I run through the commands below. It doesn't show the webpages that are generated, though.


# Start in your ggplot2 directory

# ===== Check out the ggplot2 vtest results DB from github =====
# Check it out to ggplot/visual_test/vtest/
cd visual_test
git clone git://github.com/wch/ggplot2-vtest.git vtest
ls
ls -l vtest/
cd ..

R
# ===== Install vtest =====
library(devtools)
install_github('vtest', 'wch')
library(vtest)


# ===== Run test and visualize results =====
# Run the tests on ggplot2, at ./
vtest('.')

# Generate webpages showing results
vtest_webpage()


# ===== Compare to previous results =====
# Find recent commits with saved resultsets
recent_vtest()

# Compare it to the most recent commit with saved results.
# This will print out the items that have changed
vdiffstat("06f6b3b", "")

# Generate web page showing differences
vdiff_webpage("06f6b3b", "")


# ===== Save results =====
# We didn't save the resultset from the last test when we ran it
# but we can save it now:
save_last_resultset()


If you run the tests locally, you may notice a change to some of the tick marks on log scales -- this is because I used the latest version of scales from github, which is slightly different from the CRAN version: install_packages("scales")


Please see the wiki pages and help pages for the vtest functions for more info:
https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/Visual-test-system-instructions
https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/Visual-test-system

-Winston

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: vtest screencast
parts:
Thanks, I have seen it -- I actually considered using it for visual tests early on. It would have been nice to be able to use something pre-made, but there were a number of features that ended up requiring a custom-made system.

- PNG output from R is very dependent on OS (because of fonts) and output device (png, CairoPNG, cairo, etc.), but PDF output seems to be uniform.

- The github system only lets you compare images if they've been committed to the repository, but often the purpose of the tests is to make sure everything works before committing.

- Using git as the database backend would be convenient and was discussed on the list... However, if you use a separate repo for test results, it's hard to store information like, "this set of test images goes with this commit of the ggplot2 repo". One alternative is, instead of using a separate repo, the test images could be stored in the ggplot2 repo, but this has a number of undesirable consequences, like: repo bloat,  lots of extraneous binary file changes going into commits (this would make merges difficult).

In the end I decided to implement a simple database for storing information about the tests, which is pretty easy with R. The test results don't have to be stored in a git repo. In this case, git is used, but primarily as a distribution mechanism.

-Winston
